hints: Start with test 1 with cold HCl. Think which nitrogen groups can be protonated to form a soluble salt and which cannot.
Use test 2 to decide carbonyl versus non carbonyl, then split aldehyde from ketone using test 4 and methyl ketone from other carbonyls using test 3.
Remember only a primary aromatic amine will diazotise in test 6 to couple with alkaline phenol to give an orange azo dye.
Look at test 5. Think which functional group breaks apart with hot aqueous NaOH to give two smaller products.
Combine the evidence for K and for J and L. Check why J and L give the same carbonyl results but differ from K in Fehling's and dye tests.
walkthrough:
Sort bases from non bases with HCl**
Picture what cold dilute HCl does. An amine lone pair picks up $H^+$ to give $RNH_3^+$ which is water soluble. An amide lone pair is delocalised into the $C=O$, so it is not basic enough to dissolve. J, K and L dissolve, so each contains an amine group. M is insoluble, so M has no basic amine, consistent with an amide.

Prove a C=O is present with 2,4-DNPH**
2,4-DNPH gives an orange precipitate with any aldehyde or ketone. J, K and L give the orange ppt, so each has aldehyde or ketone. M gives no reaction, so M has no aldehyde or ketone. That fits M as an amide, where the $C=O$ does not respond in the same way.

Separate methyl ketones with the iodoform test**
$NaOH(aq) + I_2(aq)$ gives pale yellow $CHI_3$ only with $CH_3CO$ group. J and L give the pale yellow ppt, so J and L each contain a methyl ketone, $RCOCH_3$. K gives no reaction, so K contains a carbonyl that is not a methyl ketone.

Pin down the aldehyde with Fehling's**
Warming with Fehling's solution gives a red $Cu_2O$ ppt only with an aldehyde. Only K gives the red ppt, so K contains an aldehyde, $RCHO$. J and L give no reaction, confirming they are ketones, not aldehydes.

Use the azo dye test for aromatic amine and hydrolysis for amide**
Diazotisation followed by coupling with alkaline phenol gives an orange azo dye only with a primary aromatic amine, $ArNH_2$. Only K gives the dye, so K contains an aromatic amine. J and L give no dye, so their amines must be aliphatic, either $RNH_2$, $R_2NH$ or $ArNHR$. Heating with $NaOH(aq)$ breaks an amide by hydrolysis. Only M reacts to give two products P and Q, so M is an amide.

Final answer: J: amine (aliphatic amine) and methyl ketone.
L: amine (aliphatic amine) and methyl ketone.
K: primary aromatic amine and aldehyde.
M: amide (no amine, no aldehyde or ketone).

hints: Focus on test 5 where M plus hot NaOH gives two smaller molecules P and Q. Think what bond to carbon is split by water with base.
walkthrough:
Recognise bond breaking by water**
You heat M, which you have identified as an amide, with aqueous $NaOH$ and one molecule splits into two smaller molecules P and Q. That is classic breaking of the $C-N$ amide link by water, promoted by base, so call it hydrolysis.
Final answer: Hydrolysis (alkaline hydrolysis of the amide).

hints: Write the general alkaline hydrolysis: $RCONHR' + NaOH \rightarrow RCO_2Na + R'NH_2$. Decide which fragment keeps the benzene ring from the formula $C_9H_{11}NO$.
Use the given formulas $C_6H_7N$ and $C_3H_5O_2Na$ to assign the nitrogen containing product and the oxygen containing product.
walkthrough:
Split the amide into amine plus carboxylate**
Under hot $NaOH(aq)$: $$\text{RCONHR' + NaOH} \rightarrow \text{RCO}_2\text{Na + R'NH}_2$$ One product contains N, the other contains $CO_2Na$. Here P is $C_6H_7N$, so P must be the amine. Q is $C_3H_5O_2Na$, so Q must be the carboxylate salt.

Fit the formulas to aniline and propanoate**
$C_6H_7N$ with a benzene ring can only be $C_6H_5NH_2$, phenylamine. That leaves a $C_3$ acid fragment from the $C_9$ parent, which as a sodium salt $C_3H_5O_2Na$ is $CH_3CH_2CO_2Na$, sodium propanoate. Together they account for $C_9H_{11}NO$ plus $NaOH$, confirming M is $C_6H_5NHCOCH_2CH_3$.

Final answer: P is phenylamine (aniline), $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$.
Q is sodium propanoate, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{Na}$.

hints: Count atoms. Each isomer has one benzene ring ($C_6H_5$) plus $C_3H_6NO$ side chain. Think where N and O can sit to make the groups found in (a).
For M use the hydrolysis products in (b)(ii) to join $C_6H_5NH$ to $COCH_2CH_3$ as an amide.
For J and L both need $COCH_3$ plus an aliphatic amine. Think of two different carbon skeletons that both keep $COCH_3$ intact.
For K you need $ArNH_2$ plus $CHO$, with a chiral carbon somewhere in the side chain. Place the $NH_2$ on the ring and build a $CH(CH_3)CHO$ side chain.
Mark chirality. Look for a carbon with four different groups. Remember only two of the four isomers are chiral.
walkthrough:
Build M first because hydrolysis tells you the join**
M gives $C_6H_5NH_2$ plus $CH_3CH_2CO_2Na$. Reverse the hydrolysis by joining them as an amide: $$\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NHCOCH}_2\text{CH}_3$$ This is N-phenylpropanamide. It has no $C=O$ that gives DNPH in the normal aldehyde or ketone way, no basic amine, and no chiral carbon, matching all tests.

Build L as the chiral methyl ketone amine**
L needs $COCH_3$ and an aliphatic $NH_2$ and must be chiral. Put both on the benzylic carbon: $$\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{-CH(NH}_2\text{)-CO-CH}_3$$ The marked $CH$ is bonded to $C_6H_5$, $NH_2$, $COCH_3$ and $H$, four different groups, so it is chiral. This gives a methyl ketone for iodoform and DNPH, an aliphatic amine for HCl solubility but no dye.

Build J as the achiral methyl ketone amine**
J needs the same groups as L but must be the achiral partner, since only two isomers are chiral and K and L will be those two. Separate N from the chiral carbon by using a secondary amine: $$\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{-NH-CH}_2\text{-CO-CH}_3$$ No carbon has four different groups, so J is achiral but still gives DNPH, iodoform, HCl solubility and no Fehling's and no dye.

Build K as the aromatic amine aldehyde**
K needs $ArNH_2$ for the dye test and $CHO$ for Fehling's and DNPH, but no $COCH_3$. Keep $NH_2$ on the ring and put an aldehyde in the side chain with a chiral centre: $$\text{H}_2\text{N-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-CH(CH}_3\text{)-CHO}$$ The $CH(CH_3)$ carbon is bonded to aryl, $CH_3$, $CHO$ and $H$, so it is chiral. This explains solubility in HCl, DNPH positive, Fehling's positive, iodoform negative and dye positive.

Check formulas and chirality count**
Each structure is $C_9H_{11}NO$ with one benzene ring. J and M have no stereocentre. K has one stereocentre at $CH(CH_3)CHO$ and L has one at $CH(NH_2)$, giving exactly two chiral isomers as stated. Always draw the chiral carbon with wedges or with an asterisk to show the centre clearly.

Final answer: J: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NHCH}_2\text{COCH}_3$ (achiral).
K: $\text{H}_2\text{N-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-CH(CH}_3\text{)CHO}$ with chiral centre at $\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)}$ shown.
L: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH(NH}_2\text{)COCH}_3$ with chiral centre at $\text{CH(NH}_2\text{)}$ shown.
M: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NHCOCH}_2\text{CH}_3$ (achiral).
Only K and L show a chiral centre (*).

hints: Think what $C_7$ aromatic sodium salt can form when the side chain is fully oxidised and then neutralised with NaOH.
walkthrough:
Identify the benzoate salt**
Strong oxidation strips the aliphatic side chain back to a $CO_2H$ group directly on the ring, giving benzoic acid, $C_6H_5CO_2H$. In alkaline work up this is neutralised to its sodium salt: $$\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CO}_2\text{H + NaOH} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CO}_2\text{Na + H}_2\text{O}$$ So W is sodium benzoate, $C_6H_5CO_2Na$.
Final answer: W is sodium benzoate, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CO}_2\text{Na}$.
